summary:
Nauru repealed the criminal-code provisions that prohibited consensual same-sex conduct in 2016, a change reported on 29 May 2016. The sections struck out belonged to a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, and the same repeal covered the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. Consensual same-sex intimacy between adults is not a prosecutable offence under Nauruan law, and a visitor should not expect prosecution on that basis.

Marriage and union recognition is a separate matter. Same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal in Nauru, and there is no recognition route for a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex.

Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and that lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex people have no employment-discrimination protection. Nauru's most recent CEDAW state report, submitted in 2016, contained no LBTI-specific information, so the official reporting machinery carries no account of trans people's situation in the country.

One detention-specific protection is documented. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on the basis of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity inside the regional processing centre. This instrument governs immigration detention rather than Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and it addresses non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex versus identity, special units or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Nauru's diplomatic position has at times supported sexual-orientation and gender-identity rights. In March 2011 the US Mission in Geneva published the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries, with Nauru among the signatories alongside Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others. Kaleidoscope Trust likewise records Nauru's support for the 2011 UN Human Rights Council Joint Statement.

For comparison across jurisdictions, the Vexen LGBT Equality Index published by the Human Truth Foundation in 2025 ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, against a top score of 4.88 for Germany and Spain and below most neighbouring Pacific states. This is one publication's composite index placement, not a count of incidents, and it measures an aggregated equality score rather than any trans-specific exposure.
localsOnly:
Residents share the 2016 decriminalisation: consensual same-sex conduct carries no penalty under Nauruan law, and the attempted-suicide offences that sat in the same 1899-derived code were repealed at the same time.

For people living in Nauru, the gaps are in recognition and protection rather than criminal liability. Kaleidoscope Trust records no explicit legal recognition or protection for intersex and transgender people, and no employment-discrimination protection for lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex workers. Same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal, so there is no domestic route to have such a relationship recognised.

Discrimination protection exists only inside the immigration-detention estate: the Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 bar discrimination on grounds including sex or gender, sexual preference and gender identity within that facility. The rules do not extend to the criminal-justice prison system, and no data documents where transgender prisoners are housed there.

Nauru's last CEDAW state report, filed in 2016, carried no LBTI-specific information, leaving residents without an official account of their situation in the treaty reporting record.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no information on whether Nauru provides any legal gender-recognition procedure for changing sex markers on identity documents or passports; the assessment that transgender people have no explicit legal recognition is an absence-of-protection finding, not a sourced statement about a specific recognition statute or its refusal.

No data was found on housing placement for transgender prisoners in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling is documented. Whether the Regional Processing Centre non-discrimination rules are enforced in practice, and how complaints under them are handled, is not sourced.

The inventory records no incidents of violence against trans people in Nauru with dates or outcomes, and no trans-specific violence rate, so no assessment of relative risk can be made from these sources.

The Vexen index placement is a single publication's composite ranking; its methodology and weighting are not sourced here, and it should not be read as a measure of trans-specific exposure.
